source_text_snippet: The thickness reduction was calculated by the formula: wt d = PA × 104 (1) where d is the depth loss (µm), wt is the weight loss (g), p the density of the steel (7.86 gcm³) and A (cm²) the surface area of the specimen. In general, the corrosion behavior of carbon steel shows striking similarities in both exposure sites. Nevertheless, the reduction in the thickness of carbon steel specimens was more pronounced in the marine environment (SITE 1). Fig. 3 reproduces the results in Fig. 2 by plotting the thickness loss against the expo- sure time in log-log coordinates. The atmospheric corrosion behav- ior of the carbon steel specimens exposed to the industrial site is observed to follow the well-known bilogarithmic equation: C = AtB (2) where C is the weight loss in terms of thickness (µm), t is the expo- sure time (months), and A, B are constants. On the other hand, the corrosion kinetics of carbon steel exposed in marine site away var- ious distances from the sea line is found to deviate from Eq. (2). The log-log plot of thickness loss versus time in this case is a discontin- uous line consisting of two linear segments. Fig. 4 shows a sche- matic weight loss versus time plot for carbon steel in marine site atmosphere in log-log coordinates. The representative equation of this irregular corrosion behavior can be described as [19]; C = At_1^(B1-B2) t^(B2) (t ≥ t_1) (3) where C is the thickness loss, A is that at the first month, t1 is the length in months of the first period of slope B1, and B2 is the slope in the second period. The slope of the second segment is obviously smaller than that of the initial segment. Furthermore, the turning points of these linear segments differ with distance from the sea line. The more distant the exposure location is from the sea line, the longer the value of the time of turning, which implies variations in the corrosion mechanism of carbon steel exposed to the marine site.

key_findings: The corrosion process of carbon steel (CS) and weathering steel (WS) is divided into two stages, with WS exhibiting a lower corrosion rate than CS throughout. The inner rust layer of WS is primarily goethite, while CS is mainly akaganeite. Rust resistance (Rr) is found to be a better indicator of rust layer protection performance than charge transfer resistance (Rt). The cathodic process of WS remains stable, whereas that of CS shows irregular evolution. Despite dense rust layer formation, chloride permeability and its destructive effects persist, with alloying elements in WS contributing to protective rust layer formation.

key_findings: The study investigated the initial stage of atmospheric corrosion on carbon steel, identifying ring-shaped and chain-type corrosion product morphologies. MnS clusters were found to be nucleation sites. Ring-shaped products consisted of lepidocrocite (y-FeOOH) and maghemite (y-Fe2O3), while chain-type products were goethite (a-FeOOH). key_findings: Atmospheric corrosion of steel in the Arabian Gulf is driven by the synergistic effects of sea-salt (chlorides) and sulphur dioxide. Initial stages involve the formation of chloride-rich blisters at anodic sites, alongside sulphates. As the rust layer thickens, chloride transport to the metal-rust interface diminishes, slowing chloride formation. In contrast, iron sulphates continue to form at the interface via an acid regeneration cycle, which is less dependent on fresh sulphate supply. The corrosion products consist of various iron oxides and oxyhydroxides, often incorporating foreign particles.

key_findings: The paper investigates atmospheric corrosion by focusing on the wetting of metal surfaces. It proposes that wetting occurs when surface relative humidity exceeds the deliquescent relative humidity of surface salts. A model for Time of Wetness (TOW) is presented, combining condensation time and rain periods. The study uses field data and ESEM to characterize surface contaminants and their wetting behavior, linking them to ISO classifications. It finds that generalized rules based on deliquescent RH and ISO classes can predict TOW with high accuracy.

key_findings: The study compared X65 pipeline steel corrosion under wet-dry cyclic and full immersion conditions. Wet-dry cycling resulted in pitting corrosion with double rust layers (porous outer, dense inner), while full immersion led to general corrosion with a thin black solid layer. Pit and groove depths followed a lognormal distribution, and maximum pit depth followed a Gumbel distribution. Corrosion kinetics for both conditions adhered to an empirical power law. Wet-dry corrosion damage surpassed full immersion after 7 days due to differences in rust layer, aeration, and chloride concentration. The diameter-to-depth ratio (DDR) decreased over time, indicating pits became narrower and deeper. Corrosion products included a-FeOOH, γ-FeOOH, Fe3O4, and Fe2O3, with γ-FeOOH showing sharp fluctuations in wet-dry cycles due to reduction.

key_findings: This study characterized marine atmospheric corrosion products on carbon steel using Micro-Raman spectroscopy and SEM/EDXA. Akaganeite was consistently detected, increasing with higher chloride deposition rates. Below a threshold of approximately 75 mg/m²/day, corrosion rates were independent of chloride deposition, with akaganeite acting as a sink for Cl-. Above this threshold, corrosion rates became dependent on chloride deposition, suggesting free Cl- accelerates corrosion. The presence of akaganeite itself was not found to increase the corrosion rate.

source_text_snippet: According to this law, absorbance is directly related to the concentration of the component in a sample and can be expressed as log(1/τ) = A = acd, where τ = transmittance, A = absorbance, a is absorption coefficient, c is concentration and d is cell thickness. Fraction of concentration of rust components was calculated taking 'a and 'c' as constants. Raman spectroscopy measurement of rust powder was carried out with Acton SpectraPro SP-2500 system. The rust powder samples were excited with the 532 nm line from Nd-YAG laser. Raman intensity ratio could also be used to calculate the concentration of components in a sample. However, this method may be prone to the errors as intensities are affected by various experimental factors, such as laser power, sample homogeneity, and sample positioning (Ref 21). The electrochemical tests were carried out using Parstat 2263 system in a Flat bottom cell consisting of a specimen, a saturated calomel electrode with saturated calomel (+0.2444 V versus SHE) and platinum wire mesh as the working, reference and counter electrodes, respectively. All the tests were carried out at room temperature in freely aerated 300 ml, 3.5% NaCl solution in which rusted surface taken after salt fog test for different durations was exposed. Initially, the OCP was measured after 1 h of stabilization followed by linear polariza- tion, which was carried out between electrode potential ranging ±20 mV versus OCP at the scan rate of 0.166 mV/s. However, for the measurement of Rp, only the linear part of potential versus current density plot within ±10 mV was used. After completion of electrochemical test and taking rust powder sample for FTIR and Raman spectroscopy, all the samples were cleaned in Clark solution consisting of 1000 ml of hydrochloric acid, 20 g of antimony oxide, and 50 g of stannous chloride (ASTM G1-03) which completely removed the rust layer from the steel surface. Corrosion rate was calculated by measuring lost weight using the following relationship (ASTM G102): Corrosion rate = W / (DAt) where W is weight loss in g, D is density in g/cm³ (=7.8 g/ cm³), A is area in cm² (=2.25 cm²), and t is time of exposure in second (s). In order to convert the corrosion rate to mm/ year, 3.15 × 10^9 is used as multiplication factor. The SEM micrographs of rusted surface of mild steel after different durations of exposure to salt fog are shown in Fig. 1, 2, and 3. Three SEM micrographs are chosen for each set with gradual increment in magnification. Rust formed on the surface was quite homogeneous and of different morphological fea- tures. Initially, fresh exposed area decreased as area covered by rust increased till 15 days (Fig. 1a, d, g, 2a, d). On the 15th day, surface was totally covered with the rust, and on the 23rd day, a fully compacted black brittle layer formed on the surface, which had subsequently chipped off on the 25th day due to expansion of inner layer exposing the sample surface again (Fig. 3f). On the 28th day, surface started re-rusting (Fig. 3g) and similar features were observed on subsequent corrosion as observed during initial days (Fig. 1). Flowery structure of lepidocrocite (γ-FeOOH) (Ref 22) was observed just after 2 days (Fig. 1c), which was the dominant constituent. As the exposure duration increased, the proportion of sharp crystalline goethite (a-FeOOH) structure (Ref 23) increased (Fig. 1f, i, 2c, f, h, 3c). Black compacted layer was formed due to the growth of whiskers of Goethite at porous locations (Fig. 2c, f, h, 4a), and porous cotton ball structure (Ref 22) was observed just beneath the upper black compacted layer (Fig. 2f, 3c), which suggested an increase in alpha-to- gamma ratio till 23 days. When the black compacted layer was removed and re-rusting started, thick plates of lepidocrocite were again observed (center location in Fig. 3i) along with sharp crystalline rods of goethite. In several locations, sandy crystals of lepidocrocite (Ref 23) (Fig. 2i) were also observed. Typical FTIR spectrum of the rusts formed on the surface of the steel during salt fog exposure is shown in Fig. 4. The presence of a-FeOOH (peaks at 885 cm⁻¹ and 790 cm⁻¹), β- FeOOH (peak at 680 cm⁻¹), γ-FeOOH (peak at 1020 cm⁻¹), and a-Fe2O3 (peak at 470 cm⁻¹) were confirmed (Ref 24). Peaks at higher wave numbers appeared due to O-H stretching and O-H bending (Ref 25). Intensity of the peak appearing at 1020 cm⁻¹ (lepidocrocite) decreased with respect to the intensity of the peak appearing at 885 cm⁻¹ (goethite) with the increasing exposure duration. This confirms the increase in ratio alpha/gamma* with fog exposure time. Alpha/gamma* ratio increased till 25 days at which lepidocrocite peak was negligible. But on the 28th day, intensity of the same peak increased sharply with decrease in alpha/gamma* ratio (Fig. 4). Beta phase was also equally present as alpha phase till 28th day. Table 1 shows the recorded values of transmittance peak intensities for different phases present in the rust with different exposure durations. Figure 5 shows the typical Raman spec- troscopy patterns of the rust samples. The peaks of a-FeOOH, β-FeOOH, γ-FeOOH, and a-Fe2O3 were clearly identified corroborating the FTIR observations (Ref 26). Intensity ratio of alpha to gamma* phase followed the same variation as in FTIR with exposure duration. The peak at 380 cm⁻¹ verified the presence of β-FeOOH although the intensity was very low. Table 2 shows the variation of electrochemical properties of the rusted surface of the mild steel after salt fog exposure for different durations. The OCP gives the information about thermodynamic stability of the sample surface in a particular corrosive environment (Ref 27). This potential varies with time due to change in the oxidation tendency of the surface. After immersion of sample in 3.5% NaCl solution for 1 h, the OCP values of all the pre-rusted samples were almost stable, and the stable OCP value was considered. The OCP increased (shifted to less negative value) until the 23rd day followed by a decrease after the removal of compacted layer (Fig. 6). Initially, the OCP increment rate was high, and the rate decreased with the number of exposure days, and it became almost constant after 15 days (Fig. 6). The highest value of the OCP was on the 23rd day, after which it again decreased. Figure 7 shows the relation between the overpotential and corrosion current density for different samples exposed to salt fog for varied durations. The slope at the corrosion potential (overpotential = 0) gives the value of linear polarization resistance (Ref 28) as per the following relation: Rp = (ΔE / Δi) E=Ecorr where AE is the change in the overpotential and Ai is the change in the current density. Linear polarization resistance Rp, which is inversely related to the corrosion rate, gives the information about rate of reactivity of the surface with the environment. Initially, Rp decreased until 10 days (137.9 to 82 2 cm²) due to the decrease in anodic to cathodic area because of formation of non-uniform rust as observed in Fig. 8. Once an uniform rust layer formed (after 15 days), it again increased and followed the same trend as the OCP (Fig. 8). On the 23rd day, the highest value of Rp (2500 Ω-cm²) was recorded, and the lowest value was 65.3 Ω cm² on the 25th day due to exposure of damaged surface followed by an increase again on the 28th day due to repassivation on the fresh exposed surface. Corrosion rate verified the electrochemical data as it decreased with exposure duration and after chipping off of the outer black compacted layer (i.e., 23rd day) it again increased (Fig. 9). Hence, the rust layer acted as a protective cover, which resisted the surface interaction with the environ- ment until a critical thickness reached after which rust layer became non-adherent. On the other hand, the rust layers consisted of several hydroxides and hydrated oxides of Fe, which offered different levels of protection to the underlying metal surface. They also form sequentially. Even there could be phase transition from one phase to another depending on the moisture, pH level, temperature, and oxygen. A few researchers have explained the phase transition of the rust constituents. Masawa et al. (Ref 5, 6, 12) have found that rusting starts with formation of y-FeOOH in slightly acidic environment, which is easily reducible and transforms to non- reactive phase a-FeOOH. Researchers (Ref 29-31) have also studied the rusting mechanism during wet-dry cycle. Evans et al. (Ref 9, 10) suggested wet-dry-wet model. According to this model, during initial wetting process iron dissolution is balanced by reduction of lepidocrocite. Thereafter, during partially drying process, magnetite is oxidized by oxygen, which diffuses through the pores. Reduction of lepidocrocite and oxidation of magnetite start again during re-wetting. However, non-possibility of oxidation of magnetite to lepi- docrocite was experimentally explained by Stratmann et al. (Ref 8, 11, 32). They also proposed three stages of the rust phase transition mechanism during wet-dry cycle. Initially, during wetting of dry surface, dissolution of iron (anodic reaction) is balanced by reduction of lepidocrocite (cathodic reaction). Thereafter, when wetting is stopped and once all the reducible lepidocrocite has been used up, metal dissolution rate would be limited to oxygen diffusion through the electrolyte in the pores because oxygen reduction would be the balancing cathodic reaction. During the 2nd stage, dissolution rate is very less due to resistance of electrolyte for oxygen diffusion. Finally, once the surface is fully dried, oxygen reduction reaction is very high so as metal dissolution. In this stage, reduced lepidocrocite layer and other ferrous products are reoxidized by oxygen, which result in the formation of a- FeOOH (Goethite). These cycle reactions slow down with the increasing rust thickness. In environment containing chlorides, the presence of β-FeOOH was also reported by many researches (Ref 12, 29, 32-35), which can also accelerate the corrosion. Therefore, ratio between non-reactive and reactive phases can be used to predict the extent of corrosion. Effect of mass ratio alpha/gamma* of crystalline a-FeOOH to the total mass of y-FeOOH, β-FeOOH, and magnetite in the rust layer on the corrosion rate has been reported in many literatures (Ref 12, 13, 36–38). It was found that with exposure duration, ratio increased, and corrosion rate decreased. In our present work, we also observed the inverse relationship between corrosion rate and alpha/gamma* (Fig. 9). Therefore, this ratio can be used as an index of protective ability. However, it is very important to mention that even without the removal of rust layer and rust characterization, one could understand the corrosion tendency from the Rp and OCP measurement, since the Rp and OCP are also following specific trend as observed in Fig. 8. Our present results can be explained by above discussion that potential shifted to less negative region due to the increase in the ratio of alpha to gamma*, i.e., protective ability of the rust. Polarization resistance decreased initially due to increase in galvanic coupling between lepidocrocite (reduction reaction) and metal dissolution site (oxidation reaction). Once the surface was totally covered by thin rust layer and lepidocrocite started transforming into stable goethite, reduction reaction rate decreased so as metal dissolution. But in this study, we observed that for the mild steel, rust cannot act as a protective layer after reaching a particular thickness level, where a hard brittle outer layer is formed but still oxygen could diffuse through the cracks. Non-reducible lepidocrocite still present in inner layer was oxidized by oxygen and transformed into goethite, which resulted in the growth of inner layer in the form of porous cotton ball structure of goethite (Fig. 10). Once the upper layer was removed, the OCP and Rp decreased due to exposure of fresh damaged surface contributing to the increase in corrosion rate. It is to be mentioned that the corrosion rate has started increasing just after the 23rd day (before the spallation of the rust layer). It is clear that the spallation is due to growth of inner porous rust layer (Fig. 10). This indicates that before spallation, rust layer has become non-adhesive, non- protective, and therefore, corrosion rate has increased just after the 23rd day. However, alpha/gamma* ratio could still increase as outer brittle layer still exhibits transformation. Therefore, a particular cycle or a day cannot be considered as specific demarcation. It would give a trend, and there must be an exposure duration range for the same, and here the range of 23 to 25 days is considered as the demarcation. A considerable amount of money is spent in corrosion rate measuring equipment and technologies (Ref 39). However, there are still many limitations in traditional methods to measure the accurate corrosion rate (Ref 40). These limitations involve effect of change in temperature, moisture level, oxygen concentration, etc., during service conditions. Techniques involving determination of rust composition are highly affected by these factors. These methods require destructive and complex sample preparation, which leads to the change in rust characteristic before the test. There has always been a requirement of non-destructive and fast monitoring technique, which can measure the severity of corrosion without disturbing the entire structure. The OCP measurement can be used as non- destructive way to measure the stability of metal surfaces in a corrosive environment. On the other hand, linear polarization can also be performed on the application site easily. Similarly, little bit of rust can be taken without disturbing the entire structure or without taking the steel sample out of the application site, and the rust can be analyzed. In our present work, we tried to correlate the change in rust constituents with OCP and Rp after exposure of the mild steel samples in cyclic salt fog environment, and a specific trend has been obtained between rust composition, the OCP and Rp with exposure time (Fig. 8). Higher the alpha/gamma* ratio, higher are the OCP and Rp and subsequently lower is the corrosion rate. Therefore, the onsite rust information, and OCP and Rp measurement can give qualitative health of the mild steel in quick time. It would at least talk about the stability of the rust layer against corrosion effect, and it can give suitable solution to the possibility of corrosion prevention too. However, it requires extensive data analysis of the steel in the actual sites with the environment it is exposed to. Finally, the present work clearly shows that the OCP and Rp of the rusted steel have unique correlation with the rust constituents and the correlation follow a specific trend with the corrosion rate. 4. Conclusions The strong correlation between variation in the corrosion rate and proportion of different phases present in the rusts formed on the mild steel surface exposed in salt fog environment with the OCP and Rp was established. With the exposure durations, the index of passivity of rust, i.e., mass ratio of alpha/gamma* (goethite/(lepidocrocite + akaganeite + hematite)) increased till the 25th day and then again decreased due to flaking off of outer brittle rust layer. The OCP and Rp of the rusted surface also follow a specific trend as both increased with the increasing mass ratio of alpha/gamma*. Similarly, the corrosion resistance also increased with the increasing mass ratio of alpha/gamma*. Therefore, measurement of the OCP and Rp can be used as a fast, non- destructive, and reliable way to assess the health of the corroding steel.

key_findings: The study establishes a correlation between Open Circuit Potential (OCP), Linear Polarization Resistance (Rp), and rust formation on mild steel in a salt fog environment. Rust composition, particularly the alpha/gamma* ratio (goethite/(lepidocrocite + akaganeite + magnetite)), influences OCP and Rp values. Higher alpha/gamma* ratios correlate with increased OCP and Rp, indicating better passivity and lower corrosion rates. The chipping off of the outer brittle rust layer leads to a decrease in OCP and Rp, signifying increased corrosion. This suggests OCP and Rp measurements, combined with rust characterization, can serve as a non-destructive method for assessing steel corrosion.

source_text_snippet: The results presented in Section 3 show that there were differences in the corrosion behavior of AISI 4135 steel exposed to different marine corro- sion zones. However, the more obvious differences were mainly reflected in the corrosion behavior of the steel under wet-dry cycle conditions (i.e., the atmospheric, splash, and tidal zones) and immersion conditions (i.e., the immersion zone). For example, the steel was characterized by pitting corro- sion under wet-dry cycle conditions but by general corrosion under immer- sion conditions (Figs. 5 and 6). The mean pore access diameter of the rust layer formed under the immersion condition was larger than that of the rust layers formed under the wet-dry cycle conditions, as shown in Table 3. Furthermore, the CR of the steel under the immersion condition was far lower than that of the steel under the wet-dry cycle conditions, as shown in Fig. 14 and Table 5. Therefore, without considering the environ- mental differences between the atmospheric, splash, and tidal zones but only the wet-dry cycle and immersion conditions, it is considered that the corrosion mechanisms of steel under these two conditions may be quite dif- ferent. It is generally accepted that the corrosion of steel under wet-dry cycle conditions is an electrochemical process that consists of a series of simulta- neous oxidation and reduction reactions (Gong et al., 2020). For a fresh steel surface, the main anodic reaction during the initial corrosion stage can be expressed as. Fe → Fe2+ + 2e- Simultaneously, as a possible electron acceptor, dissolved oxygen in the electrolyte layer is reduced to equilibrate anodic Reaction (2), where the ca- thodic reaction is depicted in Reaction (3). O2 + 2H2O + 4e- → 4OH- Therefore, the total corrosion reaction of steels in the initial corrosion stage under wet-dry cycle conditions can be described as follows (Liu et al., 2019): 2Fe + O2 + 2H2O → 2Fe(OH)2 In the initial corrosion stage, there was only a small amount of corrosion products. It is well known that the thickness of the surface electrolyte layer controlled by wet-dry cycles plays a critical role in determining the CR (Liu et al., 2019; de la Fuente et al., 2016). On the one hand, the thickness of the electrolyte layer affects the rate of oxygen transfer to the steel sur- face, thereby indirectly controlling the steel CR. On the other hand, as the electrolyte layer evaporates, when a high ohmic resistance is pro- duced owing to an excessive reduction in the thickness of the electrolyte layer, the anodic dissolution reaction of iron is restricted or even suspended. Therefore, the periodic wet-dry alternation of the steel surface causes a variation in the steel CR and ultimately leads to a com- plex corrosion state. The activation energy and surface state at different positions on a steel surface are somewhat different owing to the presence of inclusions and de- fects on the steel surface. In this case, micro-batteries are formed on the sur- face of the steel under an electrolyte layer, leading to the pitting corrosion tendency of the steel surface in the initial corrosion stage. Indeed, the thick- ness of the electrolyte layer at different positions on the steel surface is non- uniform, particularly in the later stage of the drying phase, where the de- gree of this unevenness is infinitely magnified. The difference in the thick- ness of the electrolyte layer directly determines the differences in the oxygen concentration, salts concentration, and conductivity of the electro- lyte layer. Accordingly, for electrolyte layers with different thicknesses, it is easier to form concentration cells between different positions on the steel surface, which further intensifies the pitting corrosion of the steel. Therefore, it can be considered that under the dual action of corrosive media containing chloride ions and periodic wet-dry cycles, the formation of micro-batteries and concentration cells triggers the pitting corrosion of steel. The corrosion evolution models of steel under the marine wet-dry cycle and immersion conditions are shown in Fig. 15. Once the initial pits are formed under the thin electrolyte layer contain- ing chloride ions, the pits will develop rapidly under the "autocatalytic ef- fect" (Fig. 15), resulting in obvious pits, as shown in Figs. 5(a-c) and 6(a- c). The relevant reactions in the autocatalytic process are as follows (de la Fuente et al., 2016): Fe2+ + 2Cl− → FeCl2aq FeCl2aq + 2H2O → Fe(OH)2 + 2HCl Meanwhile, owing to the sufficient oxygen supply in wet-dry cycles, the initial corrosion product is transformed into relatively stable rust phases im- mediately according to reaction (7). 4Fe(OH)2 + 4OH− + O2 → 4γ-FeOOH + 2H2O With the formation of a thin rust layer on the steel surface, the corrosion process enters a new stage, where the corrosion mechanism of the rusty steel is significantly different from that of fresh steel under the same wet- dry cycle conditions. Earlier studies have shown that the corrosion process of rusty low-alloy steel in a single wet-dry cycle occurs in three stages: wet- ting of the dry surface, the wet surface, and drying of the surface (Gong et al., 2020; Evans and Taylor, 1972; Dillmann et al., 2004). Previous stud- ies (Evans and Taylor, 1972; Stratmann, 1987; Stratmann and Streckel, 1990) indicated that the anodic dissolution reaction is largely balanced by the reduction of ferric species rather than by oxygen reduction during the wetting stage, and possible reduction reaction, that is, the reduction of γ-FeOOH, has been proposed. γ-FeOOH + H+ + e− → γ-FeII(OH)2 In the wet stage, once the lepidocrocite is used up, oxygen reduction reaction (3) is the main cathodic reaction. In this case, however, the diffu- sion of oxygen in the rust layer is difficult because it must diffuse through a thick rust layer via tortuous pores of nanometric width (refer to N2 ad- sorption analysis results in Table 3) (Hoerle et al., 2004). Therefore, in the wet stage, the corrosion of steel with an already-formed rust layer is controlled by oxygen diffusion. During drying of the surface, the thickness of the electrolyte layer gradually decreases, which facilitates the diffusion of oxygen into the rust layer, leading to a higher CR in the earlier phase of the drying stage. At the same time, the "reduced lepidocrocite" can be reoxidized to lepidocrocite under conditions of sufficient oxygen (Hoerle et al., 2004). 4γ-FeII(OH)2 + O2 → 4γ-FeOOH + 2H2O As the corrosion progresses, the rust layer gradually thickens and de- laminates (as shown in Figs. 7 and 9), accompanied by the transformation of the rust phases. In this case, compared to the outer rust layer, the evapo- ration effect of the electrolyte in the inner rust layer is relatively weak. Therefore, under the action of deposition, chloride ions are enriched in the inner rust layer and at the surface of the steel substrate after multiple wet-dry cycles (Fig. 7). Meanwhile, owing to the hydrolysis of Fe2+, Fe3 +, and other corrosion products, an acidic environment at the interface is easily formed. Eventually, a high Cl− concentration and low pH environ- ment facilitates the formation of ferrous hydroxychloride [β-Fe2(OH)3Cl] and GRI [FeIIFeIII(OH)8Cl·nH2O], which act as intermediates and ulti- mately transform into the β-FeOOH phase (Remazeilles and Refait, 2007; Alcantara et al., 2017). Briefly, the entire transformation process leading to the formation of β-FeOOH can be described as follows: FeCl2 → β-Fe2(OH)3Cl → GRI (Cl−) → β-FeOOH Because β-FeOOH is more easily formed in an environment with a high chloride ion concentration and low pH value, it is more prone to exist in the inner rust layer formed under the wet-dry cycle conditions (Evans and Taylor, 1972). This distribution characteristic of β-FeOOH were also con- firmed by our Raman analysis, in which the characteristic peaks of β- FeOOH were observed many times in the spectra of the inner rust layers, as shown in Figs. 9(b-d). After a long period of exposure, as the corrosion of steel becomes a relatively stabilized process, part of the γ-FeOOH can dis- solve into amorphous iron oxyhydroxide and turn into goethite via solid- state transformation (Jia et al., 2020). γ-FeOOH → FeOx(OH)3−2x → α-FeOOH Furthermore, both the XRD results and Raman analysis (Figs. 8 and 9) showed a relatively high content of Fe3O4 in the corrosion products formed in the different corrosion zones. On the one hand, γ-FeOOH and β-FeOOH are less stable and can be reduced to Fe3O4 by reacting with Fe2+ according to the following reactions (Jia et al., 2020; Ishikawa et al., 1998; Tanaka et al., 2014): 2γ-FeOOH + Fe2+ → Fe3O4 + 2H+ 2β-FeOOH + Fe2+ → Fe3O4 + 2H+ On the contrary, Fe3O4 may also be produced directly from the metal (Refait et al., 2016). 3Fe + 4H2O → Fe3O4 + 8H+ + 8e− Therefore, these two sources of magnetite explain why magnetite is abundant and widely distributed in the rust layers (Figs. 8 and 9). The corrosion of steel in the immersion zone can be explained by an oxygen-absorbing corrosion mechanism (Gong et al., 2020), which is sum- marized by Reactions (2)-(4). Owing to the relatively stable corrosion envi- ronment in the marine immersion zone, the corrosion process of steel is primarily affected by the rust layer (Melchers and Jeffrey, 2005). Under the immersion condition, although surface defects or inclusions can still cause an uneven distribution of potential on the steel surface, the germina- tion of corrosion pits caused by defects or inclusions is largely inhibited and eliminated by corrosion reactions that occur evenly on the steel surface (Fig. 15). Therefore, no evident pitting corrosion phenomenon was ob- served on the steel substrate in the immersion zone (Figs. 5 and 6). During the initial corrosion stage, the diffusion of oxygen through the water layer to the surface of the steel was almost unimpeded. Gong et al. (Gong et al., 2020) showed that the corrosion products formed in the initial 240 h under the immersion environment had no protective ability through elec- trochemical impedance spectroscopy test. Therefore, it can be considered that the corrosion process in the initial corrosion stage was under activation control. Nevertheless, the duration of the corrosion process controlled by activation is not long owing to the generation of corrosion products. As cor- rosion progresses, corrosion products gradually accumulate on the steel surface, forming a rust layer, which, combined with the water layer, hin- ders the diffusion of oxygen to a certain extent, and the corrosion process changes from activation control to oxygen diffusion control (Melchers, 2003). 4.2. The electrochemical corrosion process evolution in different corrosion zones In Section 4.1, the corrosion mechanism of AISI 4135 steel under the wet-dry cycle conditions was discussed, ignoring the environmental differ- ences between the atmospheric, splash, and tidal zones and the influence of other factors. However, for steel exposed to these zones, although all the steel surfaces are in an alternating wet-dry state, there are significant dif- ferences in the frequency of the wet-dry cycles and surface wetting time. These differences precisely determine the degree of corrosion and the cor- rosion progress of steel in the different corrosion zones (Alcantara et al., 2017). Changes in the wet-dry state of the surface of steel exposed to the atmospheric zone are mainly controlled by the condensation of salty aero- sols affected by RH and temperature, as well as water condensation. The thickness of the formed electrolyte layer is typically less than 100 μm (Hoerle et al., 2004). Similarly, although steel exposed to the splash zone is exposed to the marine atmosphere most of the time, it is also subjected to periodic wave splashing. However, steel exposed to the tidal zone actually experiences both the wet-dry cycles and immersion environments in a single tidal cycle. Therefore, the corrosion mecha- nism of steel in the tidal zone should be a mixed corrosion mechanism consisting of the corrosion mechanisms of steel under a wet-dry cycle and immersion conditions. Under this differentiated alternating wet-dry action, the electrochemi- cal corrosion behavior of steel after being exposed to different corrosion zones for the same period of time shows some differences, as shown in Figs. 12 and 14 and Tables 4 and 5. It is well known that the polarization resistance (Rp = Rf + Rct or Rp = Ro + Ri + Rct) represents the resistance of rusted steel to corrosion, which reflects the electrochemical CR of steel in different corrosion periods; the larger the R, value, the lower the electro- chemical CR (Al-Muhanna and Habib, 2010). For steel exposed to atmo- spheric, splash, and tidal zones, the polarization resistance of the steel tested on the 7th day was much greater than that on the 36th day. This in- dicates that the corrosion characteristics of AISI 4135 high-strength steel under the wet-dry cycle conditions, that is, the CR of steel, increased with increasing exposure time. This corrosion characteristic of AISI 4135 high-strength steel under wet-dry cycle conditions may be attributed to two reasons. On the one hand, with the thickening of the rust layer, the water-holding capacity of the rust layer was further enhanced, which pro- longed the corrosion time of the steel in the wet stage, thereby accelerating the corrosion of steel (Wang and Du, 2017; Zhang et al., 2014). On the other hand, the migration of Fe2+ is closely related to the pore access diam- eter of the rust layer, and the rust layer with a smaller pore access diameter formed in the atmospheric, splash, and tidal zones (Table 3) blocked the outward migration of Fe2+ and Fe3+ produced at the metal/oxide inter- face. To maintain electric neutrality, abundant Cl− ions migrated to the inner rust layer (as shown in Fig. 7). Under the synergistic effect of a small concentration gradient between the electrolyte at the outside and in- side of the rust layer, higher Cl− content and the accumulation of Fe3+ and Fe2+ resulted in a lower pH and anodic dissolution of steel through Reactions (5)-(6) and (15)-(16). Fe3+ + Fe → 2Fe2+ Fe + 2H+ → Fe2+ + 2Had Based on the EIS test results (Fig. 12 and Table 4), it can be found that although the change trend of the steel CR (reflected by the polar- ization resistance) was similar under the various wet-dry cycle con- ditions, the CR of steel in the different corrosion zones varied significantly. The corrosion development progress of AISI 4135 steel in the atmospheric zone lagged far behind that in the splash and tidal zones, as shown in Fig. 13 and Table 5. For the steel exposed to the immersion zone, the polarization resistance of the steel changed little throughout the measurement, as shown in Table 4. Meanwhile, it can be observed from the results of the polarization curve tests (Fig. 14 and Table 5) that the CR of steel in the immersion zone was relatively low. These indicate that the corrosion of AISI 4135 steel ex- posed to the immersion zone proceeded at a relatively stable and low rate throughout the exposure period. This can be attributed to a rust layer with a large pore access diameter (Table 3) and a large concentration gradi- ent between the electrolyte at the outside and inside of the rust layer, which facilitated the outward migration of ionic corrosion products. In addition, the low CR of steel under the immersion condition indicates that the im- mersion stage had little effect on the overall corrosion of the steel exposed to the tidal zone, whereas the wet-dry cycle stage determined the CR and progress of the steel.

source_text_snippet: Long-term predictions of metal corrosion losses (C) are performed using the power function [1]: C = C₁ τⁿ and/or the equation in logarithmic form [2-7]: log C = log C₁ + n log τ where C₁ is the corrosion loss over the first year, n is a coefficient that characterizes the protective properties of the corrosion products, and t is the test duration. Eq. (1) was suggested in a GOST (USSR State Standard) for accelerated determination of corrosion loss of metals, with indication of possible n range in various types of atmospheres [25]. It was first used to predict the corrosion losses of metals for up to 20-25 years in various regions of the world [26]. Experimental C₁ values as well as n values calculated from a stochastic relationship with C1, n = f(C₁), were used [26]. The metal corrosion loss over the first year of exposure is an integral parameter of atmosphere corrosivity. Taking into account that experimental data of short-term tests or tests without intermediate specimen withdrawals were available at that time, the relationships obtained had to be revised subsequently. Based on an analysis of results obtained in long-term tests, it was found that the kinetics of metal corrosion loss under atmospheric conditions obeys a power-linear function [27]: a power law at the initial stage assuming a parabolic increase in metal corrosion loss during the first ten years of exposure, and a linear law for exposures longer than 10 years, as it is specified in standards [28,29]. It has been shown [30] that the linear increase in corrosion loss at the stationary stage can be represented as: C = C₀ + ατ

key_findings: Corrosion of mild steel contaminated with NaCl can initiate and sustain at relative humidities (RH) as low as 33%, significantly below the bulk deliquescence RH (DRH) of NaCl (76%). At 53% RH and above, corrosion rates are comparable to those observed above the DRH. Initiation below DRH is attributed to adsorbed water on NaCl crystals in contact with steel and capillary condensation. Sustainment and significant corrosion rates below DRH are governed by the hygroscopic behavior of corrosion chemistry (anolyte and catholyte) that develops at anodic and cathodic sites, which have lower effective DRHs. Attack morphology changes from localized shallow pitting at lower RH to more sparse and deep pits at higher RH, influenced by the extent of catholyte spreading.

source_text_snippet: Background: Marine atmospheres are the most corrosive, primarily because they contain sea salts. To assess the category of atmospheric corrosivity, the deposition rate of chloride ions should be measured by experimental methods for at least I year, which requires significant expenses and is not always feasible due to the time frame required for the design and erection of structures. Methods: In this study, a fairly simple model for predicting the chloride deposition rate in the coastal zone depend- ing on the wind pattern of the test site, namely wind direction, average speed, and duration in each wind speed range, the dis- tance from the coastline, and the magnitude of marine aerosol generation for each wind speed range, has been developed. The results of comparing the calculated chloride deposition rates with experimental data obtained by the 'wet candle' method are presented. Significant findings: The applicability of the model for predicting the categories of atmospheric corrosivity toward typical metals (carbon steel, zinc, copper and aluminum) using dose-response functions has been demonstrated.

source_text_snippet: The study investigates the exceptional corrosion resistance of ancient Indian iron artifacts, revealing advanced metallurgical strategies that contributed to their longevity. Key examples include the Delhi Iron Pillar (c. 400 CE), Dhar Iron Pillar (c. 1010-1053 CE), and the iron beams of the Sun Temple in Konark (c. 1250 CE), which exhibit remarkable atmospheric durability despite centuries of exposure. The findings highlight the crucial role of high-phosphorus and low-sulfur content in promoting the formation of protective iron-hydrogen phosphate hydrate layers, passivating the metal surface and mitigating corrosion. Advanced analytical techniques, including micro-XRD, Raman spectroscopy, and SEM-EDS, identify a multi-phase corrosion system comprising amorphous δ-FeOOH (misawite), goethite (α-FeOOH), magnetite (Fe3O4), lepidocrocite (γ-FeOOH), and akaganeite (β-FeOOH). These corrosion products form layered protective structures akin to those found in modern weathering steels. Environmental factors such as humidity, temperature, and chloride exposure significantly influence corrosion behavior. For instance, while the Delhi Iron Pillar benefits from Delhi's arid climate, the iron clamps at Deogarh Temple (c. 600 CE) and the Thanjavur Cannon (seventeenth century) demonstrate resilience in high-humidity, salt-laden environments. The Adi-Mookambika Iron Pillar at Kollur exemplifies outstanding corrosion resistance in a coastal setting. Its moderate phosphorus content fosters the formation of a stable, magnetite-rich protective oxide layer, limiting moisture infiltration despite prolonged exposure to monsoon rains and saline winds. The pillar's ferrite-pearlite microstructure, combined with extensive hammer forging, enhances structural integrity by reducing oxidation pathways. This comparative analysis confirms that the corrosion resistance of ancient Indian iron was a deliberate outcome of material selection, forging techniques, and environmental adaptation. The findings provide valuable insights into modern alloy design, corrosion-resistant material development, and heritage conservation. Future research should focus on long-term corrosion modeling, microstructural analysis of lesser-characterized artifacts using advanced techniques such as atom probe tomography, and the application of ancient metallurgical principles to contemporary materials engineering for the development of sustainable, durable alloys.

Electrical resistance R depends on resistivity p and geometric parameters of the metal track, that is, thickness t, length I and width w [40]. R = p l / (w x t)

For a metal track of given resistivity and length, the evolution of electrical resistance over time directly reflects the cross-sectional loss of the material caused by corrosion and conver-sion of an electrically conductive metallic material into non- or low-conductive corrosion products. It can therefore be easily interpreted in terms of the actual corrosion depth and corro-sion rate.

Together with the geometrical parameters of the track, R depends strongly on temperature [44]. To eliminate the tem-perature effect, one part of the sensor (sensing track) is ex-posed to the corrosive environment, and its resistance is affected by both temperature variations and material loss due to corrosion, while another (reference) track is protected during exposure, and its resistance changes only due to tem-perature variations.

The actual corrosion depth (CD) of the actively corroding sensing track can then be calculated as
CD = tinit ( Rref, init / Rsens, init · Rref / Rsens )
where tinit is the initial thickness of the metal track; Rref.init and Rsens,init are the initial reference and sensing track resistances; Rref and Rsens are actual reference and sensing track resistances [11, 25, 40, 45].

key_findings: The study investigates the degradation of anti-rust oil (ARO) films on mild steel in humid atmospheres. ARO effectively intercepts saline droplets, with sodium petroleum sulfonate (SPS) transforming water molecules from free to bound states, reducing corrosivity. However, excessive saline intrusion, particularly from (NH4)2SO4 and NaHSO3, destabilizes water-in-oil micelles. Theoretical calculations indicate that intermolecular forces between water clusters and metal ions enhance electrostatic repulsion between SPS sulfonic groups, destroying the emulsion and increasing corrosion risk. An empirical model predicts thickness loss based on temperature, humidity, and salt concentration.

key_findings: Akaganeite, a destructive corrosion product, forms during atmospheric corrosion induced by NaCl deliquescence within 12 hours in an 85% RH environment. The process is characterized by isolated, discontinuous electrolyte droplets around NaCl particles, ensuring high chloride concentrations and sufficient oxygen supply, which are crucial for akaganeite formation. Initial corrosion products like lepidocrocite and magnetite accelerate akaganeite formation, and the amount of deposited salt significantly influences its macroscopic presence. Prompt removal of deposited salts is suggested to prevent akaganeite formation in marine atmospheric environments.

key_findings: The study compares X100 steel corrosion in dry/wet cycling and immersion. Dry/wet conditions show faster initial corrosion and thicker rust layers due to high Cl-, O2 diffusion, and rust layer wetness. Its mechanism involves three stages: thin liquid layer formation, O2 diffusion/Cl- concentration control, and rust layer hindering. Immersion corrosion is an oxygen-absorbing process where the rust layer offers no protection. Rust layer composition differs, with β-FeOOH in dry/wet cycling accelerating early corrosion, while α-FeOOH increases compactness later, reducing corrosion rate.

key_findings: This study presents a novel experimental setup for real-time monitoring of atmospheric corrosion of carbon steel under multi-droplet conditions using an Electrical Resistance (ER) sensor and optical microscopy. A refined signal filtering protocol (Savitzky-Golay) is used to extract corrosion rates from ER signals, minimizing thermal noise. Droplet geometry, size distribution, and contact angle are analyzed from top-view images, providing insights into electrolyte evolution. Corrosion rate shows a strong correlation with relative humidity, especially at later stages, and is influenced by droplet geometry and surface roughness. The corrosion mechanism under droplets appears to be Evans-type, with propagation primarily perpendicular to the surface. The approach aims to develop more accurate mechanistic and kinetic prediction models for atmospheric corrosion.
